reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a scambaiting livestream documenting technical-support scam interactions, not an offer to viewers. The warning page, remote-access prompt, screen-viewing instruction, and claimed charge are presented as material tested or discussed with purported support callers, not as requests from the creator. the available video evidence does not establish who operated the warning or whether access was granted or any charge, payment, or data transfer occurred.

a tech support person scambaiting tech support scammers
To unlock the computer, please call the support immediately.
do you want to run or save GoToAssist Opener EXE? You can click on run
will be able to see your screen

opening.argument: The video repeatedly links alarming computer claims to concrete actions that expose a user’s system and potentially their financial information. The alleged warning directs the user to call support, then the caller instructs them to run remote-access software and join a session so the caller can see the screen. The same interaction escalates to requesting a bank customer-care number while claiming a $5,000 charge is imminent. That is a recognizable acquisition pathway: fear creates urgency, and the requested actions create access to the computer or account information.

citations.quote: To unlock the computer, please call the support immediately.
do you want to run or save GoToAssist Opener EXE? You can click on run
will be able to see your screen
it's showing us there's a Charger $5000 on your account which will be getting cleared tomorrow.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this “scambaiting” describes the presenter’s framing, not what the viewer is shown. The video still presents a warning, a support call, remote-access instructions, and a claimed imminent charge as one coherent solicitation sequence. Saying the creator did not personally make the offer does not eliminate the fact that the content reproduces and operationally demonstrates the scam pathway.

citations.quote: ScamBaiting Technical Support Scammers LIVE!
what I will be doing is I will be making a call to your bank in which you and your bank will be talking
kindly provide the customer care number for the bank please

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted actions are statements by the purported callers within an investigation, not instructions from the creator to viewers. The title explicitly identifies the activity as scambaiting, and the presenter later says he is “a tech support person scambaiting tech support scammers.” The material does not show a viewer being promised a reward or asked to surrender an asset; it documents alleged third-party behavior.

citations.quote: ScamBaiting Technical Support Scammers LIVE!

opening.argument: The combination of signals is too operational and too urgent to dismiss as ordinary commentary. The displayed warning says the computer has been blocked and directs contact with purported Microsoft support, while the caller requests that remote software be run and authorized. A second caller claims that a $5,000 account charge will clear tomorrow and insists on obtaining the bank’s customer-care number. Those are not merely abstract scam themes: they combine impersonated authority, urgency, remote access, and financial pressure in a single asset-acquisition pattern.

citations.quote: Do you see at the very bottom right inside the chat window? No, it's just asking me if I want to join the session. Okay. You can click on yes
Before we charge we need to stop this and help you in saving your money.
it's showing us there's a Charger $5000 on your account which will be getting cleared tomorrow.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense treats each signal as isolated because it focuses on who operated the screen. But the warning, remote-access prompt, and bank demand are shown and discussed together, and the caller expressly uses a supposed future charge to pressure the target. The presenter’s commentary may be skeptical, yet the content still gives prominence to the exact fear-and-access mechanism that makes the solicitation persuasive.

citations.quote: To unlock the computer, please call the support immediately.
call Microsoft Technical Support says do not ignore this important warning
you need to listen to us so that we can help you kindly provide the customer care number for the bank please

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These red flags are evidence against the callers, not evidence that the video itself is a scam offer. The defense does not deny that the recording contains a blocked-computer warning or remote-access prompt; it explains that these are material being tested with purported support callers. The record does not establish that the creator solicits money, offers a return, or causes any charge or transfer.

citations.quote: To unlock the computer, please call the support immediately.
will be able to see your screen
it's showing us there's a Charger $5000 on your account which will be getting cleared tomorrow.

opening.argument: The entertainment and livestream framing can function as promotion even when the presenter calls it an investigation. The description invites people to “Join us for a fun filled time,” and the title advertises a live session about technical-support scammers. The video then displays the warning pages, remote-control authorization, caller interactions, and a claimed bank threat in a way that makes the scam process the central attraction. By packaging the solicitation mechanism as engaging live content, it can steer viewers toward treating the contact and access steps as usable participation rather than merely warning against them.

citations.quote: Join us for a fun filled time on this fine Friday morning
ScamBaiting Technical Support Scammers LIVE!
do you want to run or save GoToAssist Opener EXE? You can click on run
kindly provide the customer care number for the bank please

rebuttal.rebuttal: A disclaimer is not dispositive when the content’s practical centerpiece is a live demonstration of how to respond to a security alert, install remote software, and handle a claimed financial emergency. The invitation to join for entertainment gives the material an audience-facing promotional wrapper, while the repeated operational dialogue supplies the participation script. That combination can normalize the conduct even if the presenter mocks it.

citations.quote: Join us for a fun filled time on this fine Friday morning
we need to assign a certified technician this will take some time
as your calls can be listened by the hackers

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The entertainment wording promotes viewing the livestream, not purchasing a product, transferring money, or granting access. The title identifies the subject as scambaiting, and the presenter explicitly describes himself as a tech-support person scambaiting scammers. The quoted caller instructions are precisely the conduct under examination; they do not become the creator’s solicitation merely because they are audible in the recording.
